Terminology in the oil industry is always bewildering.

For example:
Arab Light crude is not really a light crude

API can mean
A) a measure of oil density 
B) American Petroleum Institute
C) Application Programming Interface

Crackers can mean
A) catalytic crackers (FCCs, RFCCs)
B) steam crackers (for petchem)
<however rarely mistaken for hydrocrackers or thermal crackers surprisingly>

Condensate can mean
A) a very light crude
B) water produced in the heating process of boilers

Sourcing enough electricity for data centres

Global electricity consumption by data centres nearly doubled in five years between 2020 and 2025, and is expected to almost double again by 2030, which will require large amounts of additional generation. 

Data centres accounted for just 1.5% of global electricity consumption in 2025 and the share is forecast to remain well below 5% through 2030 under all scenarios modelled by the International Energy Agency (IEA).  

But data centres are strongly clustered in a small number of countries, and within them a small number of regions, a pattern that is expected to persist in the medium term. 

Most of the forecast growth in data centres over the next five years is set to occur within existing clusters, which will intensify pressure on electricity networks.

The IEA estimates more than half of the new data centres under construction or already announced but not yet at the building stage are located within existing clusters.

Data centres are imposing only a modest additional load on electricity system at global scale but the impact is much more concentrated and severe in local areas ...

Germany is planning to sharply expand an existing tender that pays suppliers to keep gas available for winter, in a move designed to encourage traders to fill the country’s unusually low storage sites.

The government and the nation’s gas-market manager Trading Hub Europe GmbH intend to increase upcoming tenders by 5 billion cubic meters or roughly 50 terawatt-hours, according to a person familiar with the matter. That’s enough extra gas to fill about 20% of storage.

Germany’s sites are just 56% full, the lowest seasonal level since records began in 2009. The tenders give traders an incentive to put more gas into reserves without the government buying it directly. Suppliers that sell THE an option to call on gas this winter need to ensure they can deliver it — encouraging them to inject gas into caverns now and keep it there.

Some takeaways based on the latest Kpler data:

1) Even if Riyadh brings ~50% of pipeline flows back online quickly per their guidance, Red Sea export availability is going to remain heavily capped given Western coast inventories. 

They’ll want to avoid run cuts at domestic refineries in the West, so if refiners get first dibs on crude allocations, export stems out of Yanbu get squeezed even further. 

Riyadh is backed into leaning even harder on Ras Tanura/Juaymah, where liftings were already ramping up. Naturally the upper bound of how many physical barrels they can actually flush out hinges entirely on safety through the Strait.

2) Like I’ve been pounding the table on, more crude is actively forcing its way through Hormuz. It’s an undeniable, objective fact at this point—satellite imagery, proxies, tenders all point to the exact same thing. Anyone still denying this isn’t even worth engaging.

3) Bahri was already quietly throwing in the towel on the Red Sea and redeploying tonnage toward the Gulf of Oman anyway. That structural repositioning should provide some breathing room against tonnage crunches. Offers a bit of a silver lining for the Saudis.
